misnomer

mis-NOH-mer · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Misnomer is a name or label that is inaccurate or unsuitable for the thing it describes.

Calling a peanut a 'nut' is actually a misnomer, since it's really a legume that grows underground, more closely related to beans and peas.

Example

Tour guides love pointing out that 'koala bear' is a misnomer, since koalas are marsupials and aren't bears at all.

A misnomer isn't a lie -- it's a name that stuck around even after people learned it doesn't actually describe the thing accurately.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

misnaming: A misnaming is the act of calling something by the wrong name -- a slip someone makes in the moment, like a teacher misnaming a student on the first day. A misnomer is the wrong name itself once it has stuck: an established label that keeps misdescribing the thing it names.

mislabeling: Mislabeling is the act of attaching an inaccurate label, usually to a product or file -- a jar of walnuts mislabeled as pecans. A misnomer is not the act but the name: a label the world keeps using even though it does not fit, the way a 'shooting star' is no star at all.

Where it sits · how big the underlying error is

nickname → misnomer → fallacy

nickname vs. misnomer: A nickname is just an informal alternate name, which may or may not be misleading -- a much lighter issue than a true misnomer.

fallacy vs. misnomer: A fallacy is an entire piece of flawed reasoning, a bigger problem than a misnomer, which is only a single wrong label.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — mis-: wrongly, badly (Old French mes-)

root — nomer: name (Latin nomen, nominare)

Put it together: Misnomer combines mis- ('wrongly') with nomer (Latin nomen, 'name') -- literally 'wrongly named,' which is exactly what a misnomer is: a name or label that doesn't accurately describe the thing it refers to.

Use the root in a new word: nominate: Half the class wanted to nominate Priya, but she kept shaking her head.

Word Choice

Misnomer is specifically about a wrong name or label -- it's a much smaller, narrower problem than a truism (an obviously true statement) or a full logical fallacy (a whole flawed argument).
